title: Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic back a shared robots.txt AI training signal
content:
Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Anthropic back a shared robots.txt AI training signal
A new policy token in robots.txt lets site owners set one AI training preference across major AI providers, though rollout timing varies and the signal isn't enforceable.
On October 30, 2026, Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Anthropic announced support for a new AI training preference signal. The signal leverages an existing web standard for bot crawling preferences, robots.txt, to specify which parts of the site can be used to train models. Instead of specifying a token (aka User-Agent) for each AI training bot, these companies have agreed to use and honor a single token.
That means sites can use the new __usage_ai-training token versus having to use Google-Extended, GPTBot, and Claudebot. It also means Bing now has an option it didn't have before; you had to allow Bing to train your site if you wanted to appear in its search results.
The new robots.txt rule looks like this, with an example disallowing AI training on the entire site except for content in the /press-kit/ folder.
All four companies are still keeping their existing proprietary tokens alongside the new shared one. More importantly, the new shared token doesn't work for all companies yet. Anthropic is the only company using it today. OpenAI plans to implement it in the coming months. Microsoft will start honoring the new preferences in February 2027, and Google plans to support it sometime in early 2027.
In Google’s announcement, it said that if a site opts out with the policy token and doesn't specify Google-Extended, Google will treat it as if the site had disallowed Google-Extended. OpenAI also said it will honor the voluntary signal and encouraged other AI providers to do the same.
Microsoft went a bit further, in what feels like a non-standard, Internet Explorer-like move, by introducing DisallowExtended, which applies only to Microsoft's own experiences, like Copilot and 365. However, nothing stops other companies from using it for their own purposes in the future.
Still, not everything is settled yet. The working group's attachment draft, written by Gary Illyes of Google and Martin Thomson of Mozilla, uses a new Content-Usage HTTP header and robots.txt rule instead. Additional approaches are also being considered. For example, Cloudflare has introduced the Content-Signal directive, which uses ai-train, ai-input, and search values. The RSL Collective also launched the Really Simple Licensing standard in 2025, letting publishers set terms for AI bots.
For now, sites must keep using different tokens and methods to block AI training. Additionally, they must also use services like Cloudflare's Bot Mitigation service if they want to stop bots that ignore and bypass site directives, like Disallow in robots.txt files.
Jon Henshaw is the founder of Coywolf and an industry veteran with almost three decades of SEO, digital marketing, and web technologies experience.

report.summary: Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Anthropic back a shared robots.txt token for AI training preferences, but rollout is staggered and the signal remains voluntary and unenforceable.
report.background: AI crawlers have moved from indexing pages for search to ingesting them for model training, forcing publishers to choose between visibility and control. For years, sites have used robots.txt to manage bots, but AI providers introduced separate tokens such as Google-Extended, GPTBot, and ClaudeBot, creating a fragmented and confusing process. The conflict is sharpest at Bing: sites previously had to allow training to remain in search results. A shared token is meant to simplify that choice and establish a common norm. It arrives amid broader debates over content licensing, crawler blocking, and competing proposals from Cloudflare and the RSL Collective. Because robots.txt relies on voluntary compliance, the announcement is as much a coordination signal as a technical standard.
key_points: The new __usage_ai-training token lets a site set one AI-training preference instead of naming Google-Extended, GPTBot, and ClaudeBot separately. Sites can still use provider-specific tokens, and all four companies are keeping theirs. The article’s example disallows training across a site except a /press-kit/ folder, showing how publishers can carve out exceptions while blocking bulk model training.

Rollout is uneven. Anthropic honors the shared token today; OpenAI says it will implement it in the coming months; Microsoft will begin honoring it in February 2027; Google plans support in early 2027. Until then, publishers must maintain multiple rules. The staggered timeline means the signal’s practical value depends on which AI crawler a site most wants to address.

The signal is voluntary and not enforceable. Sites still need bot mitigation, such as Cloudflare’s service, to stop crawlers that ignore robots.txt. Google says an opt-out via the shared token, without a Google-Extended rule, will be treated as disallowing Google-Extended. Microsoft also introduced DisallowExtended for its own Copilot and 365 experiences, adding another proprietary twist.

Competing standards remain in play. A working-group draft from Google and Mozilla uses a Content-Usage HTTP header and robots.txt rule. Cloudflare has Content-Signal with ai-train, ai-input, and search values, and the RSL Collective launched Really Simple Licensing in 2025. The shared token is therefore a pragmatic interim step, not a final settlement, and publishers should expect to support several mechanisms.
report.impact: For AI companies, the shared token lowers friction and creates a compliance norm, but voluntary adoption means bad actors can still ignore it. It may push providers to compete on trust and licensing rather than crawler behavior. Developers building sites or crawlers must support the new token alongside legacy ones, and should plan for HTTP headers and Cloudflare-style signals. Regular users may see fewer unauthorized training uses of publisher content, but also more blocked or licensed content and potentially less comprehensive models. Search visibility should remain separate, though Bing’s past coupling of search and training shows why clearer signals matter. Enforcement will still depend on technical blocking and legal pressure.
report.tools: Publishers can test robots.txt rules with Google Search Console’s robots.txt report and open-source robots.txt parsers. Watch Cloudflare Bot Mitigation and Content-Signal for enforcement beyond voluntary rules, plus the RSL Collective’s Really Simple Licensing standard. For provider-specific controls, review Google-Extended, GPTBot, ClaudeBot, and Microsoft’s DisallowExtended. Developers should also track the Content-Usage HTTP header draft from Google and Mozilla, since it may become another layer sites need to support.
